claims.text: The conventionally cast eutectic high-entropy alloy has relatively coarse lamellar spacing between its constituent phases.
Rapid solidification will reduce the alloy's interlamellar spacing.
Reduced interlamellar spacing will optimize the distribution of soft and hard phases.
The additional interfaces impede dislocation motion and thereby increase strength.
The additional interfaces promote distributed plastic deformation.
Distributed plastic deformation delays crack propagation and enhances ductility.
Rapid solidification will simultaneously increase strength and ductility relative to conventional casting.
Yield strength is expected to increase by approximately 20–40% relative to the conventionally cast baseline.
The predicted yield-strength increase will occur without sacrificing ductility and may improve ductility.
The expected outcome applies under room-temperature, quasi-static tensile loading.
The comparison should use similar alloy compositions and rapid-solidification conditions that produce a measurable reduction in lamellar spacing.
Failure to obtain an approximately 20% or greater statistically significant yield-strength increase without reduced ductility would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The central hypothesis claims increased ductility, but the predicted outcome and falsification rule permit unchanged ductility. Thus, an experiment showing increased strength with no ductility improvement could satisfy the stated test while failing to establish the central simultaneous-improvement claim.
